title: Anesthesia Billing Unit Calculation
problem: Anesthesiologists must calculate reimbursement for every case using a complex formula: base units (CPT code) + time units (minutes/15) + modifying units, multiplied by the conversion factor. Errors lead to underbilling or claim denials. With the 2025 conversion factor dropping 2.83% to $32.3465, accurate calculation is even more critical to avoid revenue loss.
who: Anesthesiologists in private practice and group practices handling their own billing

skill_spec.name: Anesthesia Billing Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates anesthesia reimbursement from CPT code base units, time units, and modifiers using the current CMS conversion factor

inputs.name: modifiers
inputs.label: Modifiers (e.g., AA, QK, QZ, AD, P1-P6)

inputs.name: additional_units
inputs.label: Additional modifying units (e.g., physical status P3+)

skill_spec.formula_hint: Total units = base_units + time_units + modifying_units; Reimbursement = total_units * conversion_factor * modifier_percentage (AA=100%, QK=50%, QZ=100%)

example_queries: Calculate reimbursement for CPT 00740, 90 minutes, modifier AA, physical status P3
How much will Medicare pay for a 2-hour anesthesia case with base units of 6?
What's the billing for a QK-modified case, CPT 00300, 45 minutes?

title: Weight-Based Anesthesia Drug Dosage Calculation
problem: Anesthesiologists must rapidly calculate precise drug dosages based on patient weight, age, renal/hepatic function, and comorbidities for induction, maintenance, and emergency medications. Dosing errors are a leading cause of anesthesia-related adverse events. Manual calculation under time pressure in the OR increases risk of mistakes that can cause patient harm or death.
who: All practicing anesthesiologists, especially during emergencies and pediatric cases

skill_spec.name: Anesthesia Drug Dosage Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates weight-based dosages for common anesthesia induction, maintenance, and emergency drugs with adjustment factors

inputs.name: drug_name
inputs.label: Drug name (e.g., propofol, succinylcholine, rocuronium, fentanyl)

inputs.name: ideal_body_weight
inputs.label: Ideal body weight (kg, for obese patients)

skill_spec.formula_hint: Propofol induction: 1.5-2.5 mg/kg IV; Fentanyl: 1-2 mcg/kg; Succinylcholine: 1-1.5 mg/kg; Rocuronium: 0.6-1.2 mg/kg; Ketamine: 1-2 mg/kg IV

title: Preoperative Assessment and ASA Classification
problem: Before every surgical case, anesthesiologists must conduct a systematic preoperative evaluation: review medical history, medications, allergies, airway assessment, labs, and assign an ASA physical status classification. Missing a step can lead to intraoperative complications, cancelled cases, or malpractice claims. There is no standardized quick-reference for the complete assessment workflow.
who: All anesthesiologists, especially residents and those covering unfamiliar cases

skill_spec.name: Preoperative Anesthesia Assessment Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Systematic preoperative evaluation checklist with ASA classification guidance and red flags
steps: Step 1: Review patient medical history (cardiac, pulmonary, hepatic, renal, neurological conditions)
Step 2: Review current medications - identify anticoagulants, MAOIs, herbal supplements requiring hold
Step 3: Allergy assessment - document all drug allergies and type of reaction
Step 4: Airway assessment - Mallampati score, thyromental distance, neck mobility, dental status
Step 5: Review laboratory results - CBC, BMP, coagulation studies, ECG, chest X-ray as indicated
Step 6: NPO status verification - clear liquids 2h, light meal 6h, full meal 8h
Step 7: Assign ASA Physical Status Classification (I-VI)
Step 8: Assess anesthesia-specific risks - difficult airway, MH susceptibility, PONV risk
Step 9: Develop anesthetic plan - GA vs regional vs MAC, monitoring needs
Step 10: Informed consent - risks, alternatives, plan discussed with patient
warnings: Warning: Stop anticoagulants per protocol - verify with surgical team
Warning: Family history of malignant hyperthermia requires trigger-free technique
Warning: Obstructive sleep apnea patients need post-op monitoring plan
Warning: Document Mallampati score and backup airway plan for all patients
regulatory_refs: ASA Practice Advisory for Preanesthesia Evaluation

example_queries: What's the complete preoperative assessment checklist before a general anesthesia case?
Patient is on warfarin and needs surgery in 3 days - what should I check?
How do I classify a diabetic patient with controlled hypertension on ASA scale?

title: Malignant Hyperthermia Crisis Management
problem: Malignant hyperthermia (MH) is a rare but life-threatening emergency triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. Mortality without rapid treatment exceeds 70%. Anesthesiologists must recall a complex multi-step protocol under extreme time pressure. Even experienced providers can miss critical steps during the chaos of an MH crisis, leading to patient death.
who: All anesthesiologists, OR staff, anesthesia residents

skill_spec.name: Malignant Hyperthermia Emergency Protocol
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step MH crisis management protocol based on MHAUS guidelines with drug doses and team assignments
steps: Step 1: STOP all triggering agents immediately (volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine)
Step 2: Hyperventilate with 100% O2 at high fresh gas flows (10+ L/min)
Step 3: Call for MH cart and extra help - assign roles
Step 4: Administer dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV bolus - repeat every 5 min up to 10 mg/kg
Step 5: Mix dantrolene: each vial (20mg) requires 60mL sterile water - WARM water only
Step 6: Active cooling: iced IV saline, ice packs to axillae/groin, cooling blanket
Step 7: Treat hyperkalemia: calcium chloride 10mg/kg, insulin + glucose, sodium bicarbonate
Step 8: Monitor: arterial line, core temp, ETCO2, ABG every 10 min, urine output
Step 9: Treat arrhythmias - NO calcium channel blockers with dantrolene
Step 10: Contact MHAUS Hotline: 1-800-644-9737
Step 11: ICU admission for 24-72h monitoring - MH can recur
Step 12: Dantrolene 1 mg/kg IV every 4-6h for at least 24 hours post-event
warnings: Warning: NEVER use calcium channel blockers with dantrolene - risk of fatal hyperkalemia and cardiovascular collapse
Warning: Change anesthesia circuit and CO2 absorber if possible
Warning: Goal temperature 38.5C - stop active cooling to avoid hypothermia
Warning: Send blood for CK levels every 6h for 36h post-event

example_queries: Patient's ETCO2 is rising rapidly and temp is 39.5 during a GA case - what do I do?
How much dantrolene do I give for a 70kg patient with suspected MH?
What labs do I need to monitor after a malignant hyperthermia episode?

skill_spec.one_liner: Estimates Medicare anesthesia revenue based on case volume, case mix, and current conversion factor with year-over-year comparison

inputs.name: modifier_mix
inputs.label: Modifier distribution (% AA, QK, QZ, AD)

title: CMS Anesthesia Compliance and Audit Preparation
problem: Anesthesia practices face CMS audits for Medicare billing compliance, including proper documentation of medical direction (QK modifier), supervision ratios, and time documentation. Non-compliance with 42 CFR 482.52 and NCCI policies results in claims recoupment, penalties, and potential exclusion from Medicare. Many anesthesiologists don't know all the documentation requirements until they fail an audit.
who: Anesthesia group practice owners, compliance officers, billing managers

skill_spec.name: CMS Anesthesia Billing Compliance Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Comprehensive compliance checklist for Medicare anesthesia billing, medical direction, and documentation requirements
steps: Step 1: Verify medical direction ratio - physician directing no more than 4 concurrent cases (QK modifier)
Step 2: Confirm 7 required medical direction activities are documented for each case
Step 3: Verify start/stop times documented to the minute for all anesthesia cases
Step 4: Confirm correct modifier usage: AA (personally performed), QK (medical direction), QY (direction of one CRNA), AD (supervision 5+ concurrent), QZ (CRNA without direction)
Step 5: Verify physical status modifier (P1-P6) documented and supported by medical record
Step 6: Check that pre-anesthesia evaluation is documented and signed before induction
Step 7: Confirm post-anesthesia evaluation documented within 48 hours
Step 8: Verify anesthesia record includes all required elements per CMS guidelines
Step 9: Audit sample of claims for correct CPT code selection and base unit assignment
Step 10: Review CRNA documentation for compliance with state scope-of-practice laws
Step 11: Verify no separate billing for services bundled into anesthesia (per NCCI edits)
Step 12: Maintain audit trail and corrective action documentation
warnings: Warning: Medical direction requires documentation of ALL 7 conditions per CMS - missing even one invalidates the QK modifier
Warning: Concurrent case overlap must not violate the 4:1 ratio at any point during the case
Warning: Post-operative E&M services related to surgery are NOT separately reportable except for critical care
regulatory_refs: CMS NCCI Medicare Policy Manual Chapter 2

title: Difficult Airway Management Protocol
problem: Failed airway management is the leading cause of anesthesia-related brain injury and death. When a difficult airway is encountered unexpectedly, anesthesiologists must rapidly navigate the ASA Difficult Airway Algorithm with multiple decision points. Under stress, critical steps are missed, alternative devices are not tried in the correct order, and the decision to perform a surgical airway is delayed. Having a structured protocol instantly accessible saves lives.
who: All anesthesiologists, especially those in emergency and trauma settings

skill_spec.name: Difficult Airway Management Protocol
skill_spec.one_liner: ASA Difficult Airway Algorithm with decision tree, device sequence, and surgical airway criteria
steps: Step 1: Recognize difficult airway indicators - Mallampati III/IV, limited mouth opening, short TMD, obesity, neck immobility
Step 2: If anticipated difficult airway - consider awake intubation (fiberoptic, video laryngoscopy)
Step 3: Direct laryngoscopy attempt #1 - optimize position (ramping, BURP maneuver), use bougie
Step 4: If failed - switch to video laryngoscope, limit to 3 total attempts
Step 5: If failed VL - insert supraglottic airway (LMA, i-gel) for oxygenation
Step 6: Call for help - activate difficult airway response team
Step 7: If cannot intubate, CAN ventilate via SGA - consider waking patient vs proceeding with SGA
Step 8: If CANNOT intubate, CANNOT ventilate - declare emergency, prepare surgical airway
Step 9: Surgical cricothyrotomy - identify CTM, vertical skin incision, horizontal membrane incision, insert 6.0 cuffed tube
Step 10: Post-event documentation and notification - document all attempts, devices used, plan for future anesthetics
warnings: Warning: Limit total intubation attempts to 3+1 (3 by primary, 1 by most experienced available)
Warning: Maintain oxygenation between attempts - SpO2 must recover before next attempt
Warning: Do NOT delay surgical airway in CICV scenario - brain damage begins in 3-5 minutes
Warning: Document difficult airway in patient chart and provide MedicalAlert bracelet information
regulatory_refs: ASA Practice Guidelines for Management of the Difficult Airway (2022 Update)

example_queries: Patient is Mallampati IV with a short neck - what's my airway plan?
Failed two intubation attempts, can ventilate with LMA - what should I do next?

title: Locum Tenens Compensation Comparison
problem: Anesthesiologists considering locum tenens work need to compare hourly rates across states, factor in travel expenses, malpractice coverage, and calculate the true annual equivalent compensation vs employed positions. With rates varying from $275/hr nationally to $375/hr in New York, and employed median compensation at $535K, the math is complex and often done on napkins. Poor analysis leads to suboptimal career and financial decisions.
who: Anesthesiologists evaluating locum tenens vs employment, those negotiating contracts

skill_spec.name: Locum Tenens vs Employment Compensation Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Compares locum tenens hourly rates to employed positions factoring in benefits, taxes, and expenses for anesthesiologists

inputs.name: benefits_value
inputs.label: Estimated annual benefits value (health, retirement, CME)

skill_spec.formula_hint: Locum gross = rate * hours * weeks; SE tax = gross * 15.3% (up to SS cap); Net = gross - expenses - SE_tax; Employed total = salary + benefits
